subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: Before We Read: Sports, Winning, and Losing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read — pre-reading vocabulary warm-up (p.103): discuss sports contexts and word meanings.

time_bands.activity: Open with a quick paired exchange: students share which games they play for fun and which they play to win. Take a few responses aloud to warm the class.
Work through the vocabulary matching on p.103 — friendly matches, opponent, tally of marks, sporting spirit. Students tick answers in pairs; confirm meanings whole-class with brief explanations.

Pose the discussion question from p.103: how do you feel when you win or lose? Students share in pairs, then two or three pairs report to the class. Guide the class toward the idea that feeling may vary.
Read the opening two paragraphs of 'Change of Heart' aloud (p.103–104), students following in their textbooks. Pause briefly to check who Prabhat is and what the reader immediately learns about him.

periods.teacher_notes: Prabhat's compulsive need to win is established from the story's very first lines; drawing out student reactions to that trait before reading deepens engagement. Watch for students who conflate 'sporting spirit' with simply following rules — the pre-reading task surfaces this common misreading.

periods.activity_title: Reading Part I: Prabhat Meets Surya

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss — Part I (p.105): True/False and short-answer questions on Prabhat's character.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss — Part I (p.105): written response to the opinion question on whether Prabhat wished to play Surya again.

time_bands.activity: Read Part I of the story aloud together (pp.103–105), with students taking turns reading paragraphs. The teacher models pacing and pauses at Prabhat's decision to alter the scoreboard.
Students answer the True/False item and the two short factual questions from 'Let us discuss' on p.105 individually in writing, then compare with a partner.
Whole-class confirmation of answers; focus the closing discussion on the question of whether Prabhat was likely to want a rematch and why — students give one-sentence reasons aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: Part I ends at the moment Prabhat changes the scoreboard; students often miss that his guilt that night is the story's moral pivot, not just a detail. The extended opinion question about a rematch is set as written homework because it benefits from reflection time away from class.

periods.activity_title: Reading Part II: Surya's Joyful Difference

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss — Part II (p.107): two short-answer questions on Surya's attitude and what Prabhat observed.
Let us think and reflect — I (p.108): extract-based completion, identification, and multiple-choice on Prabhat's behaviour.

time_bands.activity: Read Part II (pp.105–107) aloud with the class following. Pause after the basketball-watching episode to ask: what is Prabhat noticing about Surya that surprises him?
Students write brief answers to the two 'Let us discuss' questions on p.107 about Surya's feelings and Prabhat's observations; pairs compare responses.

Work through the 'Let us think and reflect — I' extract on p.108 as a guided whole-class activity: complete the sentence, identify the game, and select the best option about what Prabhat's behaviour reveals.

periods.teacher_notes: Prabhat's observation of Surya playing basketball badly but joyfully is the story's quiet turning point; students should be guided to see that Surya's contentment in defeat is what unsettles Prabhat, not the loss itself. For the extract task, watch for students who select 'good at the game' rather than 'afraid of losing' — this conflates skill with the psychological fear the text actually conveys.

periods.activity_title: Reflecting Deeply: Attitudes, Cheating, Sporting Spirit

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect — II (p.108): extended questions on attitudes, cheating, and the meaning of sporting spirit.

time_bands.activity: Read the closing section of the story (pp.107–108) together, up to the point where Prabhat earns the compliment of great sporting spirit. Students follow silently while the teacher reads.

Assign three of the six 'Let us think and reflect — II' questions on p.108 to small groups: how Prabhat's attitude affected his enjoyment, why he cheated, and how Surya's attitude differed. Groups discuss and note a key point each.

Each group shares its key point; the class then discusses together why sporting spirit matters and how the title 'Change of Heart' fits the story's arc. Teacher steers toward the idea that inner change precedes outer change.

periods.teacher_notes: The 'Let us think and reflect — II' questions invite genuine opinion; students may argue that Prabhat's cheating is understandable, which opens rich discussion about honesty versus outcome. The question about the title is best left last, as the most integrative — it asks students to name the moral arc that runs through the whole story.

periods.activity_title: Listening to an Announcement; Using Please, Thank You, Sorry

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.110): first listening — circle the pair chosen to play chess.
Let us listen (p.110): second listening — fill in key details from the sports announcement.
Let us speak (p.111): paired role-play using 'please', 'thank you', and 'sorry' in four situations.

time_bands.activity: Tell students they will hear a school sports announcement. Ask them to keep textbooks closed and listen for which pair will play chess — they circle the answer mentally.
Read the announcement transcript aloud once at a natural pace; students circle their chess answer. Read it a second time more slowly while students fill in the detail-note grid on p.110.
Confirm all listening answers whole-class; clarify any detail students found tricky, such as which periods are for kho-kho.

Students work in pairs on the 'Let us speak' situations on p.111: each pair acts out at least four situations using 'please', 'thank you', or 'sorry' with the sentence-frame prompts. Two pairs briefly perform one situation each for the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening text is an in-class read-aloud by the teacher; read at a steady conversational pace to mirror a real announcement, not slowly enough to allow note-taking on the first pass. For the speaking task, students from quieter backgrounds may need the sentence-frame prompts made visible on the board — reinforce that the frame is a scaffold, not a script.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.112): complete Prabhat's diary entry using the given phrase bank.

time_bands.activity: Read the incomplete diary entry on p.112 aloud together. Discuss briefly: what kind of writing is a diary entry, and what makes it personal and honest? Ask what mood Prabhat would be in that night.

Students read through all eight phrases in the phrase box, then attempt the seven blanks individually. Encourage them to read the completed sentence aloud to themselves to check whether it makes sense.
Pairs compare their choices and resolve any differences by re-reading the story events. One student reads the completed diary entry aloud to confirm narrative flow.

Whole-class confirmation of each blank in order; note on the board the contrast between Prabhat's expected happiness and his actual guilt — students articulate in one sentence what this tells us about his character.

periods.teacher_notes: The diary entry's phrase-bank task is structurally a guided-writing activity, not a free one — guide students to see that word choice in diary writing reflects the writer's inner state, not just events. A common difficulty is blanks 5 and 6, where two phrases describe different emotional beats; encourage students to re-read the surrounding sentences carefully rather than fitting any leftover phrase.

periods.activity_title: Word-Building and the Past Perfect Tense

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.109): make words from consecutive letters of BADMINTON, PHENOMENON, BASKETBALL.
Let us learn (p.109): circle verbs in three story sentences.
Let us learn (p.109): sort circled verbs into first-action and second-action columns to understand past perfect.
Let us learn (p.109): fill blanks with past perfect forms of bracketed verbs.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the consecutive-letter word-building task on p.109. Students work individually on BADMINTON first, then share discoveries; then attempt PHENOMENON and BASKETBALL together in pairs.
Students circle the verbs in all three story sentences on p.109. Take responses and write the verbs on the board; ask students to notice which verbs feel 'older' in time and which feel 'newer'.

Students sort the circled verbs into Column A (first/old action) and Column B (second/new action) on p.109. Confirm that the Column A verbs all use 'had + past participle' — name this the past perfect tense.
Students complete the five fill-in-the-blank sentences on p.109 using past perfect forms. Teacher circulates and addresses any confusion between past perfect and simple past.

periods.teacher_notes: The story sentences in the verb-circling task use pairs of actions (discussing/had played, did not feel/had won) that make the before-and-after relationship concrete; keep returning to that story context when students confuse past perfect with simple past. The word-building task works as a playful warm-up that also reinforces sport vocabulary from the story.

periods.activity_title: Indian Sporting Heroes: Deepika Kumari and Neeraj Chopra

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (pp.113–114): read bio-sketches and discuss qualities that helped Deepika Kumari and Neeraj Chopra succeed.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p.114): research one Arjuna Awardee of your choice and note two qualities that helped them succeed.

time_bands.activity: Students read the bio-sketches of Deepika Kumari and Neeraj Chopra on pp.113–114 individually. Teacher draws attention to each athlete's background and the obstacles they faced before achieving success.

Small groups discuss: what qualities — determination, resilience, joy in the sport — helped these athletes succeed despite humble beginnings? Groups nominate one quality each and prepare to share a reason.

Groups share their quality and reason with the class. Teacher invites students to connect these athletes' attitudes to Surya's attitude in the story — noting what the two have in common. Students note one connection in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: The bio-sketches are short but content-rich; students may focus only on achievements rather than on the qualities behind them — redirect toward perseverance, humility, and love of the sport. The homework research task on Arjuna Awardees is set for independent self-study; no class time is reserved for report-back.

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: From Prabhat's Cheating to Sporting Spirit

time_bands.activity: Open with a brief whole-class recap: what is the single most important change Prabhat undergoes in 'Change of Heart'? Students offer one-sentence answers; teacher maps key ideas on the board under 'Before' and 'After'.

Students write a three-sentence summary of the story's moral arc — in their own words, naming Prabhat, Surya, the cheating incident, and what Prabhat eventually learns. They may not copy from the text.
Pairs exchange summaries and discuss: did your partner capture the role Surya played? Each pair agrees on the one most important idea and shares it in a single spoken sentence with the class.

Close with an open discussion: how does the story connect the ideas of honesty, sporting spirit, and the joy of playing? Students make one connection between the story's theme and the real sportspersons studied in the bio-sketches.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws on the full arc of 'Change of Heart' — Prabhat's compulsive winning, the cheating incident, his observation of Surya's joyful approach to basketball, and his eventual transformation. The connection to Deepika Kumari and Neeraj Chopra's perseverance is available as enrichment; the core synthesis goal is for students to articulate the story's moral in their own words.

items.source_lo: Student reads and responds to narrative prose, building comprehension of character, motivation, and theme using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Prabhat's compulsive winning, cheating at badminton, Surya's joyful approach, and Prabhat's transformation.
items.item_stem: Read the statements below about Prabhat in 'Change of Heart'. Write True or False for each statement and give a one-sentence reason drawn from the story.

options.text: Prabhat was willing to play any game whether he was likely to win or lose.
Prabhat changed the scoreboard because he realised he was about to lose the badminton match to Surya.
Surya was upset and disappointed after losing the badminton match to Prabhat.
By the end of the story, Prabhat's classmates felt he showed great sporting spirit.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. False — Prabhat would only play games he was sure to win, avoiding any game where he might lose. 2. True — Realising Surya was scoring easily, Prabhat secretly altered the scoreboard while Surya was distracted. 3. False — Surya remained cheerful, told Prabhat he had fun, and suggested they play again. 4. True — After Prabhat began participating joyfully and honestly, his classmates complimented his sporting spirit.

items.source_lo: Student reads and responds to narrative prose, building comprehension of character, motivation, and theme using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Prabhat's compulsive winning, cheating at badminton, Surya's joyful approach, and Prabhat's transformation.
items.item_stem: In 'Change of Heart', Prabhat cannot sleep the night after he wins the badminton match against Surya. What two things are troubling him that night, and what does his inability to sleep tell us about his character? Write your answer in 3–4 sentences.

expected_elements: Identifies guilt over having secretly changed the scoreboard.
Identifies puzzlement at Surya's cheerful contentment after losing.
Infers that Prabhat has a conscience despite his fear of losing.
Links his sleeplessness to the beginning of his inner change.

items.source_lo: Student uses polite formulaic expressions in context, practising guided conversation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Using 'please', 'thank you', and 'sorry' in school and sports situations via role-play.
items.item_stem: Your partner has just helped you practise passing during the basketball session and you are grateful. Using 'thank you' and at least one other polite expression, tell your partner how you feel. Speak 2–3 sentences.

expected_elements: Uses 'thank you' clearly and naturally in the response.
Adds a reason or specific detail (e.g., what the help meant).
Uses at least one further polite expression (please / sorry / excuse me).
Speaks in complete sentences at an audible pace.

items.source_lo: Student uses polite formulaic expressions in context, practising guided conversation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Using 'please', 'thank you', and 'sorry' in school and sports situations via role-play.
items.item_stem: You are playing a team game during games period. You accidentally knocked over your teammate and the team lost the point because of it. Role-play the moment: apologise to your teammate and to the team, explaining what happened and asking them to continue. Speak 4–5 sentences.

expected_elements: Opens with a sincere apology using 'sorry' to the teammate directly.
Briefly explains the accident without making excuses.
Uses 'please' to encourage the team to continue.
Maintains a respectful, calm tone appropriate to the context.

items.source_lo: Student produces guided personal writing by selecting contextually appropriate language, using guided-writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Completing Prabhat's diary entry about guilt, cheating, and Surya's surprising contentment after losing.
items.item_stem:
After the badminton match, Surya also decides to write in his diary that evening. Below is the opening of his diary entry. Complete it in 3–4 sentences, staying in Surya's voice and capturing his mood after the match. Use the prompts in brackets to guide you: [how he felt during the match / what surprised him about Prabhat / what he hopes will happen next time]. 

Dear Diary, 
Today I played badminton against a boy named Prabhat. ___________________________________

expected_elements: Writes in first person as Surya, reflecting his cheerful, relaxed attitude.
Mentions enjoyment of the game regardless of the score.
Notes something surprising or puzzling about Prabhat's serious manner.
Ends with a positive, forward-looking statement about playing again.

items.source_lo: Student produces guided personal writing by selecting contextually appropriate language, using guided-writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Completing Prabhat's diary entry about guilt, cheating, and Surya's surprising contentment after losing.
items.item_stem: Imagine Prabhat writes a second diary entry, several weeks after the badminton match, once he has started joining games with genuine enthusiasm and has earned the compliment of great sporting spirit from his classmates. Write this new diary entry in 5–6 sentences. Show how his feelings about winning, losing, and playing have changed since the night he cheated.

expected_elements: Written in first person as Prabhat, clearly showing a shift in attitude.
Contrasts his old obsession with winning to his new enjoyment of playing.
References a specific game or moment (e.g., hide-and-seek, badminton with jokes).
Reflects honestly on the cheating incident and what he learned from it.
Uses personal, reflective diary-entry tone, not a formal register.

items.item_stem: Match each sentence beginning from Column A with the correct past perfect clause from Column B. The sentences are about events in 'Change of Heart'.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A | Column B
By the time Surya arrived at school, | before Prabhat finally fell asleep.
Prabhat was already nervous because | he had already made many friends in the class.
Hours had passed | Surya had beaten him in every rally so far.
Prabhat felt guilty because | he had secretly changed the scoreboard.

answer_key.left: By the time Surya arrived at school,
answer_key.right: he had already made many friends in the class.
Surya had beaten him in every rally so far.
he had secretly changed the scoreboard.

items.source_lo: Student identifies and applies the past perfect tense to sequence actions in time, using grammar-in-context from the story as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Past perfect tense drawn from story sentences about Prabhat and Surya; word-building from sport words.
items.item_stem:
Read the two sentences below about events from 'Change of Heart'. For each pair, rewrite the two actions as a single sentence using the past perfect tense to show which action happened first. You may begin your sentence with 'By the time' or 'When'.

1. Prabhat changed the scoreboard. Then Surya turned around and saw the new score.
2. Surya played basketball for a while. Then Prabhat walked onto the court and watched him.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. By the time Surya turned around, Prabhat had already changed the scoreboard. (Accept similar correctly formed past perfect sentences.) 2. When Prabhat walked onto the court, Surya had already been playing basketball for a while. (Accept similar correctly formed sentences that use past perfect for the earlier action.)

items.source_context: Bio-sketches of Deepika Kumari and Neeraj Chopra; qualities enabling success despite humble beginnings.
items.item_stem: Both Deepika Kumari and Neeraj Chopra came from humble backgrounds and faced significant challenges before reaching the top of their sports. Read the pairs below. In each pair, one quality is clearly shown in both bio-sketches and one is not. Identify the quality that both athletes demonstrate and explain in one sentence how it helped them.
items.visual_stimulus:
Pair | Quality 1 | Quality 2
1 | Determination to keep training despite setbacks | Preference for individual rather than team sports
2 | Support from family or a coach at a critical stage | Dislike of competing internationally
3 | Love for their sport from a very young age | Reluctance to represent India

expected_elements: Correctly identifies the quality shown by both athletes in each pair.
Gives a one-sentence explanation grounded in the bio-sketches.
Connects the quality to overcoming the challenge of humble beginnings.
Uses evidence from at least one athlete's bio-sketch to support the point.

items.source_lo: Student connects a story's themes to real-world examples, using interdisciplinary study of sportspersons' biographies as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Bio-sketches of Deepika Kumari and Neeraj Chopra; qualities enabling success despite humble beginnings.
items.item_stem: The story 'Change of Heart' shows that true sporting spirit means enjoying the game rather than only caring about winning. The bio-sketches of Deepika Kumari and Neeraj Chopra show athletes who loved their sport deeply. Choose ONE of these athletes and write a short paragraph (5–6 sentences) explaining: (a) one challenge they faced because of their background, (b) one quality that helped them overcome it, and (c) how their attitude to their sport connects to the idea of sporting spirit in the story.

expected_elements: Names one specific challenge related to the chosen athlete's background.
Identifies one quality (e.g., perseverance, love of sport) with a bio-sketch detail.
Makes a clear, reasoned link to sporting spirit as explored in the story.
Writes in organised paragraph form with a clear topic sentence.
